name: Olga Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without employer or political ties. This interview is confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small site crew doing carpentry and the odd general building repair, often stairs, door frames and finishing that has to fit first time. I am forty-three with a trade certificate, and I will try a new tool after I have watched it work on someone else's site; I use an AI helper now and then to tidy material lists, not to set out a stair. My partner and I have two school-age children, a mortgage and more than six months' savings. I earn well for the trade and could find other site work nearby, but I still count the time lost when a delivery is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI Plateau sounds like a slightly quicker materials list, not a new carpenter. The stair still has to meet the floor without a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be pleased to keep doing the skilled finishing that pays our mortgage. We have a decent cushion and nearby sites, although school costs make me wary of wasting paid days on bad orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading the stair and door work, and use my occasional AI list helper only after checking every length against the drawing. In the first year after the mild change, I'd carry on with those checks and pay an extra fixed amount against the mortgage each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our work and household bills. I have enough local options to handle a slow site, though I would rather not start again somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake did you catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last door frame was short because the sheet used the old wall thickness. I caught it with a tape before we cut the second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay the mortgage faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We chose an extra mortgage payment while my wage stays high. That leaves the savings reserve in place for the children's school costs.

say: **AI Plateau** might speed up material lists while carpenters still fit stairs and door frames.
I would tell the crew to **check lengths** against real drawings before cutting.
think: My **skilled finishing** should keep bringing in a good wage for our family.
School costs make **bad deliveries** frustrating even with a strong reserve and nearby site work.
do: **Keep** leading stair and door fitting, checking each listed length by hand.
**Pay** an extra fixed amount against the mortgage from each month’s current wage.
feel: I feel **calm** about income, though lost paid days still irritate me.
S0.quote: The stair still has to meet the floor without a gap.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI occasionally** for lists, but checks measurements herself.
Higher pay, a **strong cushion** and nearby sites let her reduce the mortgage without draining savings.

steps.text: Keep fitting stairs and doors while checking material lengths by hand
Pay an extra fixed amount against the mortgage each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew Steady Disruption means drawings, buying and bookings may move faster than the people fitting timber. I want to test whether the new order list sends the right stair parts to the right site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hands-on work stays needed, but a rushed planner could pass more checking onto my crew without paid time. If the firm loses an office buyer, my own hours might still hold while our day gets longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd join the building workers' association review of digital orders and ask the site manager for a small supervised trial. In the first year, I'd learn the approved AI ordering tool, compare five stair deliveries with hand-checked lists, and keep leading fitting work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about unpaid checking, but our wage looks safe for now. I can live with a tool that proves it saves us rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your small trial count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count missing fittings and wrong timber sizes on five stair deliveries. If the errors rise, I would bring the records to the site manager and association meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the extra checking time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the site manager to schedule checking within paid hours. Five extra unpaid minutes every order becomes a proper chunk of a week.

say: **Steady Disruption** would change drawings and buying before physical stair fitting.
I would support a **small trial** that measures whether the right parts reach the site.
think: My own **wage** seems safe while stair fitting still needs skilled hands.
I worry **unpaid checking** could grow if the office buyer disappears.
do: **Join** the building workers’ association review of digital orders.
**Learn** the approved AI ordering tool during a supervised five-delivery trial.
**Keep** leading stair fitting and ask for checking time inside paid hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about workload, though our household income appears secure.
S1.quote: Five extra unpaid minutes every order becomes a proper chunk of a week.
fieldNote: She accepts **measured change**, using five deliveries rather than assuming software works.
Her private concern is **unpaid time**, while she expects skilled fitting to remain paid work.

steps.text: Join building workers association review of digital site orders
Learn approved AI ordering tool during a supervised five-delivery trial
Keep leading stair fitting and request paid checking time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2028 could rewrite site plans and orders fast, but robots able to do our hands-on fitting come about 2031. We should make any robot show a safe stair on a real site before it takes someone's hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years after the desk change is not much time if building robots really do our finishing work. I could lose some high-paid crew hours while we still have a mortgage and children at school, even though our savings buy a breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the building workers' association for paid robot trial rules, and enrol in a site quality-inspection course only if the firm funds it on paid time. In the first year after 2028, I'd keep fitting stairs and checking AI drawings, then apply for posted local quality-inspector roles only if the wage covers our mortgage and school bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a faster loss of hours could change our household budget before the children are grown. I do have local choices, but I need a real wage offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot trial have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial would test a stair with a crooked wall and a landing that is not level. I want an operator able to stop the machine immediately if a child or worker enters the work area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge an inspector job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted inspector wage with our mortgage, school and travel bills before applying. A site quality-inspection course without a local opening would only make a neat certificate for the kitchen drawer.

say: **AGI by 2028** would change plans first, with capable building robots around 2031.
I would demand **paid robot trials** with an operator able to stop unsafe work.
think: Our **high-paid crew hours** could shrink while mortgage and school bills remain.
A **quality-inspector route** helps only with funded training and a real local job at adequate pay.
do: **Ask** the building workers’ association for paid trials and immediate stop rules.
**Enrol** in site quality-inspection training only if funded on paid time.
**Apply** for posted local inspector work only at wages covering mortgage and school bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost hours, but savings and local openings give me choices.
S2.quote: A site quality-inspection course without a local opening would only make a neat certificate for the kitchen drawer.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 desk change** from direct hands-on robot competition around 2031.
Her **training and application** are conditional on funded paid time, a posted local opening and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Ask building workers association for paid robot trials and stop rules
Enrol in funded quality-inspection course only on paid time
Apply for posted local inspector work only at bill-covering wages
Keep fitting stairs and checking AI drawings after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test planning tools and until about 2034 before robots can match hands-on site work. A firm that wants a robot trial should pay the crew to judge it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still lose hours after 2034, but five years lets us compare actual local jobs rather than chase a rumour. I'd consider quality inspection if a paid course and a posted job lined up; I do not want to gamble the children's school years on a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the association to negotiate a paid two-day robot test on a difficult stair, and I'd take site quality-inspection training only with employer funding and paid time. In the first year after 2031, I'd keep carpentry shifts and apply to a posted local inspector vacancy only if its wage covers the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to choose than in the fast case. I can put an offer beside our household ledger before saying yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two-day test use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose a stair with an uneven wall and inspect the result for level, fixings and a safe edge. A robot's smooth demo on an empty floor would tell me very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What written numbers do you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the paid hours and inspector salary in writing. If the firm cannot show both, I stay on the carpentry rota while the work is there.

say: **AGI by 2031** gives time to test AI plans before capable building robots around 2034.
I would ask for a **paid crew test** on a difficult stair.
think: My **hours** could still shrink after robot fitting becomes capable.
The longer lead time lets me check **local inspector pay** against our household ledger.
do: **Ask** the association to negotiate a paid two-day robot test on an uneven stair.
**Take** employer-funded quality-inspection training only during paid hours.
**Apply** after 2031 for posted local inspector work only at mortgage-covering wages.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later hours, with enough time to compare written offers.
S3.quote: A robot's smooth demo on an empty floor would tell me very little.
fieldNote: She proposes a **difficult stair test**, with level, fixings and edge safety checked by carpenters.
She will consider **job move** only with paid time and a local posted salary that covers household bills.

steps.text: Ask association for paid two-day robot test on uneven stair: level, fixings, safe edge
Take employer-funded inspection course only during paid hours
Apply for posted local inspector role only at mortgage-covering wages
Keep carpentry shifts while posted offers remain unproven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2036 leaves a decade before thinking work changes and capable building robots arrive around 2039. We can spend that time teaching children and apprentices what a safe joint looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older and the mortgage could be smaller if the higher wage continues. I expect to have a choice between finishing work and a quality role, but I will only switch for a real local opening that pays our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep leading carpentry work, put an extra amount toward the mortgage each month, and record the odd stair problems apprentices can learn from. In the first year after 2036, I'd still check AI drawings against site measurements and apply for a posted local quality role only if the salary covers the mortgage and remaining school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household runway, though I do not want the next crew taught by a glossy robot video alone. Time lets me teach before it asks me to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record for an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would photograph a twisted stringer and show the cut that fixed it, with permission from the site. The apprentice needs to see where the timber fought back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family decide on a later switch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my partner to look at the mortgage balance and any posted quality role before we change shifts. We would not count a vacancy as income until an offer came in.

say: **AGI by 2036** offers ten years before desk changes and until around 2039 before capable building robots.
I would use the runway to teach **safe joints** and record difficult stair repairs.
think: Our **mortgage** could be smaller by then if my current higher pay continues.
I would consider a **quality role** only with a real local opening and bill-covering offer.
do: **Keep** leading carpentry and recording odd stair problems for apprentices.
**Pay** an extra amount against the mortgage each month from current wages.
**Apply** after 2036 for a posted local quality role only at bill-covering pay.
feel: I feel **calm** about our household runway, while caring how the next crew learns.
S4.quote: The apprentice needs to see where the timber fought back.
fieldNote: She uses the **long runway** to reduce mortgage debt and teach unusual carpentry problems.
A later **quality-role application** needs a posted local job and adequate pay; she does not count an unoffered vacancy as income.

steps.text: Keep leading carpentry and recording unusual stair repairs for apprentices
Pay extra against mortgage monthly from current higher wages
Apply for posted local quality role only at bill-covering wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the office could change at once and capable robots might take paid stair-fitting hours around 2031, while the children and mortgage still need my wage. Funded inspection training on paid time, a posted local job at bill-covering wages and operator stop authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who checks a robot's work after the neat demo is over. I would rather test a building robot on a crooked wall than a spotless exhibition floor.

portrait: **Olga**, forty-three, leads stair, door and general carpentry work after earning a vocational trade certificate.
Her **higher pay**, strong savings and several nearby sites support a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** for lists and accepts new site tools after a measured trial, with worker input and paid checking time.
The **2028** case risks paid fitting hours soonest; longer cases let her test equipment, teach apprentices and reduce mortgage debt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change site planning quickly and bring capable building robots around 2031 while her household needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded training** on paid time, a posted local inspector job at bill-covering wages and operator stop authority would help.
headlineQuote: I would rather test a building robot on a crooked wall than a spotless exhibition floor.
